summary: IGMP is how IPv4 hosts tell neighboring multicast routers which groups they want to receive. Version 3 adds source filtering, so a host can ask for traffic only from, or excluding, specific source addresses. This internet-standard text obsoletes RFC 3376.

plainLanguage.summary: When you join a group chat, you can say "only from these people." IGMPv3 lets a computer tell its router which senders it wants to hear from.

subtitle: How IPv4 hosts tell multicast routers which groups, and which senders, they want to hear from.

tldr.problem: Multicast routers need to know which groups have listeners on each attached network. Earlier IGMP versions could only say 'send me this group from anyone', which is not enough for Source-Specific Multicast.
tldr.mechanism: IGMPv3 lets a host report a group together with a filter mode (INCLUDE or EXCLUDE) and a list of source addresses. Routers send Queries, hosts answer with Reports, and routers keep timers per group and per source.
tldr.outcome: This revision obsoletes RFC 3376 with clarifications and errata fixes, updates RFC 2236, and stays interoperable with IGMPv1 and IGMPv2.

today: RFC 9776 is an Internet Standard (STD 100) published in March 2025. It obsoletes RFC 3376 and updates RFC 2236, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What IGMPv3 Does
sections.content:
The Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP) is used by IPv4 hosts and routers to report their IP multicast group memberships to neighboring multicast routers. A router can also be a group member itself, in which case it runs both the router part and the group-member part of the protocol.

Version 1 was the first widely deployed version. Version 2 (RFC 2236) added low leave latency, meaning a shorter time for a router to learn that a group has no members left. Version 3 adds source filtering: a system can ask for packets sent to a multicast address only from listed sources, or from all sources except listed ones. This is what Source-Specific Multicast (SSM) needs.

This document obsoletes RFC 3376 with clarifications and fixes for errata, and it updates RFC 2236 because a proper IGMPv3 implementation must also handle IGMPv2 Report and Leave messages. It covers only group membership reporting, not the other IGMP management functions.
sections.plainLanguage: Older versions were like saying 'I want the newsletter'. This version lets you say 'I want the newsletter, but only from these writers', so routers do not waste effort carrying stuff nobody wants.

sections.title: Sockets, Interfaces and Filter Modes
sections.content:
The RFC describes a conceptual service interface, IPMulticastListen (socket, interface, multicast-address, filter-mode, source-list). The filter-mode is INCLUDE (receive only from the listed sources) or EXCLUDE (receive from everyone except the listed sources). An implementation MAY limit the source-list size, but the limit MUST NOT be less than 64 addresses per list, and exceeding it MUST return an error.

Each call completely replaces the earlier request for the same socket, interface and group. The old Join operation equals EXCLUDE with an empty list, and Leave equals INCLUDE with an empty list.

The system keeps state per socket and derives one record per group for each interface. If any socket is in EXCLUDE mode, the interface record is EXCLUDE with the intersection of the EXCLUDE lists minus every INCLUDE source. If all sockets are INCLUDE, the interface record is INCLUDE with the union of their lists. An implementation MUST NOT use an EXCLUDE record when all sockets are in INCLUDE state.

Queries and Reports are not subject to source filtering and must always be processed by hosts and routers.
sections.plainLanguage: Each app says what it wants. The computer then combines everyone's wishes into one short list to give the router, so the router hears one clear request per group.

sections.title: Query and Report Messages
sections.content:
IGMP messages ride in IPv4 datagrams with IP protocol number 2, an IP Time-to-Live of 1, Internetwork Control precedence, and the Router Alert option. IGMPv3 introduces two message types: 0x11 Membership Query and 0x22 IGMPv3 Membership Report. Implementations MUST also support the IGMPv1 Report (0x12), IGMPv2 Report (0x16) and IGMPv2 Leave Group (0x17). Unrecognized types MUST be silently ignored.

A Query has three variants. A General Query has a zero group address and zero sources and is sent to 224.0.0.1. A Group Specific Query names one group. A Group-and-Source Specific Query names a group and a list of sources. The Max Resp Code is in tenths of a second; values of 128 and above use a floating-point form, (mant | 0x10) << (exp + 3). The QRV and QQIC fields carry the querier's Robustness Variable and Query Interval, and the S flag tells routers to suppress their normal timer updates.

A Report is sent to 224.0.0.22 and holds one or more Group Records. Each record has a type, a multicast address and a source list. Six record types exist, in three families: Current-State (sent in answer to a Query), Filter-Mode-Change and Source-List-Change (sent when local state changes). Auxiliary data is not defined, so senders MUST set Aux Data Len to zero.
sections.plainLanguage: A Query is the router asking 'who is listening to what?'. A Report is the computer answering with a list of groups and the senders it wants or does not want.

sections.title: How Group Members Behave
sections.content:
A host does not answer a Query at once. It picks a random delay between zero and the Max Response Time, which spreads replies out and avoids a burst. Pending answers are combined where possible: one timer per interface covers General Queries, and a per-group timer covers Group Specific and Group-and-Source Specific Queries. Implementations MUST NOT send a Report immediately on receiving a General Query.

When the reception state of an interface changes, the host sends a State-Change Report immediately. Table 3 of the RFC says which records to send: for example, a change from INCLUDE (A) to INCLUDE (B) sends ALLOW (B-A) and BLOCK (A-B). To cover a lost Report, it is retransmitted [Robustness Variable] - 1 more times at random intervals within the Unsolicited Report Interval. If more changes happen first, the new difference is merged with the pending report.

Unlike IGMPv1 and IGMPv2, hosts no longer suppress their Reports when they hear another member's. The Appendix gives reasons: routers may track per-host membership, suppression works badly on bridged LANs with IGMP snooping, and removing it simplifies hosts.
sections.plainLanguage: When the router asks, each computer waits a random moment before answering, so they do not all shout at once. If a computer changes its mind, it speaks up straight away and repeats itself in case someone missed it.

sections.title: How Multicast Routers Behave
sections.content:
A router keeps state per group per attached network: a Router Filter Mode, a Group Timer and a list of source records, each with a Source Timer. An EXCLUDE group with an empty source list means all sources are wanted, which is the IGMPv3 equivalent of an IGMPv1 or IGMPv2 join. The group is in EXCLUDE mode as soon as any member reports EXCLUDE, and the Group Timer is what moves it back to INCLUDE when all EXCLUDE members go quiet.

Routers send General Queries periodically. When they receive a State-Change Record indicating a member is leaving, they send Group Specific or Group-and-Source Specific Queries, repeated [Last Member Query Count] times at [Last Member Query Interval]. Only after [Last Member Query Time] with no interested Report may the router stop forwarding. IGMP only gives the routing protocol forwarding suggestions; it does not override multicast routing information.

One querier is elected per subnet by IP address: a router that hears a General Query from a lower address stops sending General Queries and starts its Other-Querier-Present Timer.

SSM-aware routers SHOULD ignore EXCLUDE-type records for addresses in the SSM range.
sections.plainLanguage: The router keeps a notebook for each group with a countdown clock beside each sender. When a clock runs out and nobody renews it, the router stops sending that traffic.

sections.title: Working with IGMPv1 and IGMPv2
sections.content:
A Query's version is decided by its size: length 8 with Max Resp Code zero is IGMPv1, length 8 with a non-zero code is IGMPv2, and length 12 or more is IGMPv3. Anything else MUST be silently ignored.

IGMPv3 hosts MUST operate in v1 and v2 compatibility modes, tracked by a Host Compatibility Mode per interface and driven by Querier-Present timers. Routers keep a Group Compatibility Mode per group, driven by Host-Present timers. In IGMPv2 mode a router translates a v2 Report into IS_EX({}) and a v2 Leave into TO_IN({}), and ignores BLOCK records. When a group returns to IGMPv3 mode it takes time to regain source-specific state.

If any older router is present, the querier MUST use the lowest IGMP version on the network, which must be administratively assured. Implementations are RECOMMENDED to offer a setting that disables compatibility mode for SSM-only networks, disabled by default.
sections.plainLanguage: If some old gadgets on the network only speak the older language, the newer ones switch to that older language so everybody can still understand each other.

sections.title: Timers and Default Values
sections.content:
Most timers are configurable, but non-default settings MUST be consistent among all systems on a link. The key defaults are:

  • Robustness Variable: 2. It MUST NOT be zero and SHOULD NOT be one. IGMP tolerates (Robustness Variable - 1) lost packets.
  • Query Interval: 125 seconds.
  • Query Response Interval: 100, meaning 10 seconds.
  • Last Member Query Interval: 10, meaning 1 second.
  • Unsolicited Report Interval: 1 second.

Derived values include the Group Membership Interval, which MUST be (Robustness Variable times Query Interval) plus (2 times Query Response Interval), and the Other Querier Present Interval, which MUST be (Robustness Variable times Query Interval) plus (0.5 times Query Response Interval). A larger Robustness Variable helps on lossy links but lengthens leave latency, and a longer Query Interval means less periodic IGMP traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: These are the stopwatch settings: how often to ask, how long to wait for answers, and how many times to repeat before giving up. The defaults work for most networks.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
IGMP provides no confidentiality, so any device on a link can passively read its messages. The RFC walks through forged messages of each type. A forged Query from a lower IP address can make the forger the querier and, if it ignores Leave messages, keep traffic flowing to empty groups for up to a Group Membership Interval. Forged Group-and-Source Specific Queries with long source lists and large Max Response Times could exhaust a host's memory and CPU, so a host stack could limit queries per membership or record only a limited number of sources.

Against externally forged messages, routers SHOULD NOT forward Queries, and hosts SHOULD ignore v2 or v3 Queries without the Router Alert option. Forged v1 or v2 Reports can push a router into a compatibility mode that ignores Leave messages or source-specific state, which can be handled by a switch to ignore those versions entirely. IPsec in AH mode may also be used, though it applies directly only to Queries and Leave messages in IGMPv1 and IGMPv2, because Reports go to the group being reported.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone on the same network could fake a message or pretend to be the boss router. The RFC lists simple checks to catch fakes, like ignoring messages that did not arrive the right way.

fields.name: Max Resp Code
fields.desc: Maximum time allowed before sending a responding report, in tenths of a second.

fields.name: Checksum
fields.desc: One's complement checksum of the whole IGMP message.

fields.name: Group Address
fields.desc: Zero in a General Query, otherwise the group being queried.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: Managed by the IGMP Type Numbers registry.

fields.name: QRV
fields.desc: The querier's Robustness Variable, or zero if it exceeds 7.
